answer_text:
# 💜 The History of Purple: A Colour Born of Power, Poison, and Accident

---

## Origins: A Colour Scarce in Nature

Purple's rarity in nature and the expense of creating the colour gave it a supernatural aura for centuries. Our ancestors probably never saw a purple fruit, flower, bird, or fish — because purple is very rare in nature. This scarcity would go on to define everything about the colour: its cost, its status, and its mystique. The earliest purple dyes date back to about 1900 BC, and it took some 12,000 shellfish to extract just 1.5 grams of the pure dye — barely enough to dye a single garment the size of a Roman toga.

---

## The Phoenicians and Tyrian Purple

The story goes back around 3,000 years to the Phoenicians, a seafaring civilisation living along the Mediterranean coast (modern Lebanon, Syria, and Israel). Production of Tyrian purple for use as a fabric dye began as early as 1200 BC by the Phoenicians, and was continued by the Greeks and Romans until 1453 AD, with the fall of Constantinople.

The dye stemmed from the foul-smelling mucous gland of a marine mollusc. As a result, the term "purple" owes itself to the Latin word for a purple shellfish: *purpura*. It has been suggested that the name Phoenicia itself means "land of purple."

The dye was greatly prized in antiquity because the colour did not easily fade, but instead became brighter with weathering and sunlight. It came in various shades, the most prized being that of black-tinted clotted blood.

Because it was extremely tedious to make, Tyrian purple was expensive: the 4th-century BC historian Theopompus reported that "purple for dyes fetched its weight in silver at Colophon" in Asia Minor. Indeed, about 250,000 snails were required to make an ounce of purple dye.

---

## Purple and Power: Emperors, Togas, and Sumptuary Laws

The expense meant that purple-dyed textiles became status symbols whose use was restricted by sumptuary laws. The most senior Roman magistrates wore a *toga praetexta*, a white toga edged in Tyrian purple. The even more sumptuous *toga picta*, solid Tyrian purple with gold thread edging, was worn by generals celebrating a Roman triumph.

By the fourth century AD, sumptuary laws in Rome had been tightened so much that only the Roman emperor was permitted to wear Tyrian purple. As a result, "purple" became a metonym for the office — the phrase "donned the purple" means "became emperor."

Purple also featured in one of history's most famous romances. Purple even played a role in the romance of Caesar and Cleopatra. Historians tell that Cleopatra organised a party for Caesar to celebrate his victories, and the colour scheme was purple — then the most expensive dye in the world. The luxury atmosphere created was really impressive, and Caesar fell deeply in love with Cleopatra.

The production of Tyrian purple was tightly controlled in the succeeding Byzantine Empire and restricted for imperial silks. Later, in the 9th century, a child born to a reigning emperor was said to be *porphyrogenitos* — "born in the purple." The phrase "born to the purple," meaning someone born into royalty, comes from this very history.

---

## The Middle Ages and the Renaissance: Sacred and Royal

Purple maintained its image as a colour of prestige into the Renaissance, when it became a symbol of the Catholic Church's power, often seen in the robes of high-ranking clergy.

During later periods, purple held the same power: in Elizabethan Europe purple was reserved for royalty, and throughout England's Tudor period only King Henry VIII was allowed to dress in the colour; he went as far as committing an Earl to death by treason for wearing it.

Meanwhile, by the Middle Ages, Tyrian purple had started to disappear. The Byzantine Empire, which controlled the dye trade, declined. The technique of making the dye was kept secret, passed down within families, and eventually lost. Cheaper dyes, like those made from plants, became more practical. By the time of the Renaissance, the original recipe for Tyrian purple was forgotten.

---

## 1856: The Accidental Revolution

Then came one of the most celebrated accidents in scientific history. In 1856, an 18-year-old English chemist, William Henry Perkin, mistakenly invented "Perkin's Purple" — the shade we recognise today as mauveine or mauve. Perkin was at the time trying to find a cure for malaria by attempting to synthesise quinine in a laboratory. When cleaning up the solution he'd created with alcohol, he noticed he'd produced a dark purple liquid.

He initially labelled it "Tyrian purple," to capitalise on history. He soon switched to calling it "mauve," after the French name for the mallow flower.

The vibrant mauveine purple was derived from coal tar and made its creator a Fellow of the Royal Society and Royal Medallist. More significantly, his purple dyestuff marked the beginning of a revolution in organic chemistry, the birth of an industry that has since given us a rainbow of colours, as well as drugs, explosives, fertilisers, plastics, and synthetics beyond measure.

Over the centuries, the advent of synthetic dyes made purple more accessible, yet it retained its royal connotations and continued to evoke a sense of opulence and prestige.

---

## Purple Across Cultures

Purple's meaning was never universal. Japan sees purple as a symbol of nobility and strength, which can be traced back to the Heian period when purple was associated with the imperial family. Thailand views purple as somber; widows often wear it during periods of mourning. India, on the other hand, ties purple to spirituality and peace, frequently using it during religious ceremonies. In China, purple is a symbol of spiritual awareness as well as physical and mental healing.

---

## Purple as Protest and Identity

The women's suffrage movement adopted purple as a key colour. In this context, the hue symbolised dignity and justice, reflecting the struggle for equality and rights — showcasing purple's ability to unify collective aspirations. In Western cultures, people view purple as a symbol of creativity, mysticism, and pride. In the United States and Europe, it is also closely linked to the LGBTQ+ community and the fight for equality.

---

## The Psychology of Purple
